sec.p: Single-cell transcriptomic analysis in colorectal cancer identified a stem-like cell cluster with organ-specific metastatic preferences mediated through DLL4-NOTCH signaling and metabolic shifts [289]. In lung cancer, targeting carnitine palmitoyl transferase 1 A (CPT1 A) induced ferroptosis in CSCs enhances immunotherapy efficacy by disrupting a CPT1 A/c-Myc positive feedback loop that protects against oxidative stress [290]. Similarly, acute myeloid leukemia (AML) stem cells rely on ferritinophagy, mediated by NCOA4, to sustain quiescence, making iron metabolism an exploitable vulnerability [291].

In glioblastoma, CSCs exhibit unique metabolic dependencies, such as threonine metabolism fueling tumor growth through YRDC-mediated translational reprogramming, suggesting a potential avenue for dietary interventions [292]. Additionally, glioblastoma stem cells integrate into neural circuits, where cholinergic neurons drive tumor invasion, and radiotherapy further enhances neuron-tumor connectivity, implicating neuronal activity inhibition as a therapeutic strategy [293].

Long non-coding RNA (LINC00115) promotes chemoresistant breast CSC stemness and metastasis via SETDB1/PLK3/HIF1α signaling, presenting a novel target for intervention [294]. In pancreatic cancer, cancer-associated fibroblast (CAF) autophagy upregulates CD274/PDL1 expression, impairing antitumor immunity and suggesting that CAF autophagy inhibition with immunotherapy could improve treatment responses [295]. Finally, WNT5B has been identified as a driver of osteosarcoma stemness, chemoresistance, and metastasis, emphasizing the need for novel CSC-targeting therapies [296].

sec.title: Nanomedicine strategies for targeting CSCs
sec.p: Nanoparticle-mediated drug delivery and combination therapies are emerging as effective approaches for eliminating CSCs and modulating the tumor microenvironment (TME). Engineered microparticles co-loaded with tumor antigen and resiquimod (imidazoquinoline) have successfully reprogrammed tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), fostering the expansion of stem-like CD8 + T cells and enhancing anti-PD-1 therapy in hepatocellular carcinoma and melanoma models [297].

Nanomedicine has enabled novel strategies to eradicate CSCs by modulating their metabolism and immune evasion mechanisms. Cuproptosis-based nanomedicine, leveraging copper ionophores in combination with photothermal therapy, has demonstrated efficacy in suppressing triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) by eliminating CSCs and enhancing antitumor immune responses [209]. Similarly, exosome-sheathed porous silica nanoparticles co-delivering 3,3'-diindolylmethane and doxorubicin have shown promise in attenuating epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in TNBC, reducing CSC-driven malignancies [298].

The use of hydrogel-based dual-drug nanocarriers encapsulating anti-CSC agents such as salinomycin or curcumin with lauroyl-gemcitabine offers a promising approach for residual glioblastoma treatment, preventing tumor recurrence [299]. Glutaminolysis inhibition has emerged as a viable method to enhance photodynamic therapy (PDT) efficacy against CSCs by disrupting reactive oxygen species (ROS) defense, as demonstrated by nanoparticle-assisted combination therapies [300]. Furthermore, HYL001, a novel lonidamine derivative, selectively targets CSC mitochondria by blocking glutamine metabolism, exhibiting substantial antitumor activity [301].

Several natural compounds and biomimetic approaches have been explored for CSC-targeted therapies. Viridiflorol, a bioactive terpenoid, has demonstrated potent anti-neoplastic effects by inducing apoptosis in breast, lung, and brain cancer cells [302]. Additionally, nano-immuno-conjugates combining photosensitizers, gold nanoparticles, and anti-CD271 antibodies have been developed to enhance PDT against esophageal cancer stem cells, offering a promising avenue for precision medicine [303].

sec.title: Advances in nanomaterial design for CSC therapy
sec.p: Recent nanomaterial design and characterization innovations have refined CSC-targeted therapy, enabling improved drug delivery, enhanced biocompatibility, and precision targeting [304]. Stimuli-responsive biocompatible nanoparticles tailored for the TME have been developed, emphasizing the need for thorough characterization using 3D tumor spheroid models to optimize in vitro evaluation [305].

A functionalized PAMAM-based nanoformulation has been designed for targeted 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) delivery in hepatocellular carcinoma, demonstrating enhanced tumor accumulation and improved therapeutic efficiency. Similarly, metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) have been explored as multifunctional nanocarriers for drug delivery and catalytic therapy, with promising results in CSC-targeting applications [306, 307].

sec.title: Overcoming intracellular barriers and enhancing drug penetration
sec.p: Overcoming intracellular drug delivery challenges and TME-imposed barriers remains a critical area of research. A significant limitation in CSC-targeted therapy is lysosomal sequestration of therapeutic agents, which prevents drugs from reaching intracellular targets effectively [351. To address this, TME-responsive protein nanogel-platelet hybrid systems have been developed to facilitate cytosolic drug release, bypassing endosomal entrapment and ensuring efficient intracellular drug delivery [308].

sec.title: Future directions and clinical implications
sec.p: Integrating personalized nanomedicine, CSC-targeted therapies, and stimuli-responsive drug delivery systems holds immense potential for revolutionizing cancer treatment. Future research should optimize nanocarrier designs to enhance CSC targeting, improving specificity and drug payload capacity while minimizing off-target effects. Developing combination therapies that exploit CSC vulnerabilities and integrate immune modulation strategies will be crucial in overcoming resistance mechanisms. Additionally, advancing biomimetic nanomedicine to harness natural carrier systems can improve drug stability, bioavailability, and targeted delivery. Enhancing in vivo validation through clinical studies will be essential to evaluate the efficacy of nanomedicine-based CSC-targeting approaches, ensuring their translation into clinical practice. Addressing these key challenges could significantly improve cancer prognosis, reduce relapse rates, and pave the way for more effective and durable treatment strategies.

sec.title: Advanced nanomedicine techniques
sec.p: Advanced nanomedicine technologies are revolutionizing healthcare by enabling precise drug delivery, enhancing imaging techniques, and facilitating personalized treatment strategies that optimize patient outcomes. These innovations are driving the development of more effective therapies that reduce side effects while maximizing therapeutic efficacy, ushering in a new era of precision medicine (Fig. 6).

sec.title: Gene therapy based on nanoparticles (siRNA, miRNA, CRISPR)
sec.p: Gene therapy has enormous promise for treating cancer because it precisely modifies cellular functions using nucleic acids. However, efficiently delivering gene-editing tools like CRISPR/Cas to solid tumors remains a significant challenge. Researchers have looked into novel approaches to get around this, such as altering the TME and creating non-viral nanoparticle delivery systems.

Targeting the mechanics of tumor tissue to increase the effectiveness of gene editing is one promising strategy. A multiplexed dendrimer lipid nanoparticle (LNP) system that co-delivers focal adhesion kinase (FAK) siRNA, Cas9 mRNA, and sgRNA (siFAK + CRISPR-LNPs) [309]. This system significantly improved gene editing in tumor spheroids by reducing extracellular matrix (ECM) stiffness, which enhanced nanoparticle uptake and penetration. The knockdown of FAK led to a more than tenfold increase in gene editing efficiency. Additionally, using siFAK + CRISPR-PD-L1-LNPs disrupted PD-L1 expression, significantly inhibiting tumor growth and metastasis in mouse models. These findings highlight the potential of modulating tumor mechanics to improve gene editing and offer a synergistic approach for nanoparticle-based therapies [309].

Another critical strategy involves the development of stimuli-responsive non-viral nanoparticles for gene delivery. Reichel and Traeger (2023) emphasized the challenges of delivering nucleic acids, such as their high molar mass and negative charge. The success of mRNA-based vaccines has spurred the development of advanced gene transporters capable of providing various nucleic acids, including DNA (pDNA) and RNA (mRNA, siRNA, miRNA, gRNA, or ASOs). These stimuli-responsive nanoparticles enable precise gene release and expression control, enhancing therapeutic outcomes [310].

In sum, by combining mechanical modulation of the TME with advanced non-viral nanoparticle delivery systems, researchers are making significant progress in enhancing gene therapy for cancer. These approaches provide new opportunities for precise gene editing and targeted delivery, ultimately improving the potential of gene therapy as a transformative tool in cancer treatment.

sec.title: Nanomaterial-based photodynamic and photothermal therapy
sec.p: Photodynamic therapy (PDT) and photothermal therapy (PTT), two promising non-invasive cancer treatment modalities, are frequently combined to increase therapeutic efficacy. However, issues like hypoxia, drug resistance, and limited tumor targeting make the creation of advanced nanomedicines necessary. Recent research has concentrated on creating multifunctional nanoparticles that can synergistically deliver PDT and PTT to improve diagnosis and treatment monitoring. These nanoparticles frequently incorporate imaging capabilities. (Please cite references in this paragraph).

One strategy involves utilizing biomimetic nanoparticles, such as platelet membrane-camouflaged magnetic nanoparticles (Fe3O4-SAS@PLT), which trigger ferroptosis and generate mild immunogenicity, enhancing immunotherapy response in non-inflamed tumors [311]. These nanoparticles repolarize macrophages and improve the efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade therapy (Fig. 7).

sec.p: Researchers have developed various nanoplatforms to overcome the limitations of phototherapy, particularly hypoxia and thermotolerance. Lonidamine-encapsulated liposomes, for example, have been shown to enhance PDT and PTT of hepatocellular carcinoma by inhibiting glycolysis, thereby reducing oxygen consumption and heat shock protein production [312]. Similarly, BODIPY-conjugated hyaluronic acid nanoparticles (BODIPY-HA NPs) have been designed for combined PDT and PTT, utilizing self-assembly to control ROS generation and photothermal effects [274].

Upconverting nanoparticles (UCNPs) have also been explored for synergistic PDT and PTT under cold near-infrared (NIR) excitation, addressing the overheating issues associated with conventional UCNPs [313]. By utilizing Nd3 + -sensitized UCNPs, researchers have achieved enhanced ROS generation and improved cancer cell inhibition.

Furthermore, facet engineering of nanomaterials, such as Cu7S4 nanosheets, has demonstrated promise in efficient photothermal and photodynamic synergistic antibacterial therapy, demonstrating the versatility of these approaches beyond cancer treatment [314].

Advanced nanomedicines, such as aggregation-induced emission (AIE) photosensitizer nanoparticles (NP-DBD), have been developed for targeted tumor therapy and NIR-II fluorescence imaging, enabling bioorthogonal-guided activation of the cGAS-STING pathway and robust immune modulation [315].

Combination therapy has been further enhanced by integrating radiotherapy with PDT and PTT. For instance, copolymer-coated liquid metal nanoparticles (RGD-PEG-PAA-MN@LM) have been designed for synergistic photothermal, photodynamic, and radiation therapy of liver cancer, demonstrating improved tumor inhibition [316].

To address the challenges of glioblastoma treatment, researchers have developed IR820-conjugated reduced graphene oxide quantum dots (rGOQD) that alleviate tumor hypoxia and inhibit heat shock proteins, enhancing the efficacy of PTT and PDT [317].

Multisubcellular organelle-targeting nanoparticles, such as FA-BSA/Cu/NQ/IR780/DOX NPs, have been constructed for synergistic chemotherapy and photodynamic/photothermal tumor therapy, demonstrating multifunctional properties, including fluorescence imaging capabilities [318].

Polydopamine-based nanoparticles (PDA-ZnPc + Nps) loaded with photosensitizers have also been investigated for synergistic PDT and PTT, demonstrating remarkable efficacy and minimal systemic damage [319].

Plasmonic Bi nanoparticles encapsulated by N-carbon (Bi@N-Carbon@PEG-DOX) have been developed for dual-imaging and photothermal/photodynamic/chemotherapy, integrating imaging and synergistic therapy in one nanoplatform [320].

Tyrosinase-activated nanocomposites (IOBOH@BSA) have been developed for double-modals imaging-guided photodynamic and photothermal synergistic therapy of melanoma, utilizing tyrosinase as a biomarker for selective imaging and ablation [321].
Finally, near-infrared and lysosome-targeted BODIPY photosensitizers have been designed for photodynamic and photothermal synergistic therapy, demonstrating enhanced therapeutic effects [322].

These studies underscore the significance of multifunctional nanomedicines and synergistic therapeutic approaches, as well as the variety and inventive approaches being investigated to improve PDT and PTT for cancer treatment.

sec.title: Theranostic nanoparticles: combining therapeutics and diagnostics
sec.p: In cancer research, the creation of theranostic nanoparticles with combined therapeutic and diagnostic properties has accelerated significantly. Because this approach allows for real-time drug delivery and therapeutic response monitoring, these nanoplatforms hold promise for personalized medicine. Biomimetic approaches utilizing cell membrane coatings, enhance biocompatibility and prolong circulation time, improving targeted drug delivery [323]. For instance, red blood cell membrane-coated nanoparticles (TT-RBC-NPs) have promise in breast cancer treatment, demonstrating enhanced cytotoxic efficacy and specific binding to cancer cells [323].

The enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect has been a guiding principle in nanomedicine development; however, recent studies have emphasized the need to go beyond the EPR effect to improve tumor targeting and treatment efficacy [146]. Strategies such as active targeting using specific ligands and tuning nanoparticle properties for optimal tumor accumulation are being explored.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is crucial in theranostics, enabling non-invasive visualization of nanoparticle distribution and therapeutic effects. Ultrasmall theranostic nanoparticles have been developed to enhance MRI contrast and amplify radiation dose, improving local control in radiation therapy [324]. For example, in preclinical models, AGuIX-Bi nanoparticles, with tailored Gd/Bi ratios, have demonstrated enhanced DNA damage and tumor growth inhibition [324]. Furthermore, iron-functionalized mesoporous polydopamine nanoparticles (MPDAFe NPs) have been shown to combine efficient drug delivery with MRI capabilities, demonstrating significant cytotoxicity toward cancer cells [325].

Combining MRI and computed tomography (CT), bimodal imaging offers complementary diagnostic information. Fe3O4@Au nanoparticles have been developed for bimodal CT and MRI imaging, showing significant tumor and tumor blood vessel enhancement [326]. Additionally, fullerene nanocrystals and gold nanoparticle hybrids (FGNPs) have been investigated relative to photoacoustic imaging and photothermal therapy, demonstrating strong photoacoustic signals and photothermal heating characteristics [327].

Targeted theranostic nanoparticles have been designed for specific cancer types, such as triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), utilizing ICAM1-targeting to enhance diagnostic and therapeutic efficacy [328]. These nanoparticles, loaded with gadolinium and doxorubicin, have demonstrated promising results in cell-based and tumor model-based experiments.

Beyond cancer, theranostic nanoparticles are being explored for other diseases, such as acute ischemic stroke. pH-responsive multifunctional theranostic rapamycin-loaded nanoparticles have been designed to deliver rapamycin to ischemic brain tissues, demonstrating acid-enhanced MRI and near-infrared fluorescence imaging [329].

Localized delivery of theranostic nanoparticles and high-energy photons using microneedles-on-bioelectronics has been developed to overcome the limitations of conventional delivery methods, particularly for brain tumors [330]. This approach enables precise delivery of nanoparticles and high-energy photons, enhancing photodynamic therapy and chemotherapy.

Gold-in-gold cage nanoparticles have also been investigated for photothermal ablation and photoacoustic imaging in biofilm-associated infection models, demonstrating a strong biocidal effect against bacterial biofilms [331]. These studies highlight the diverse applications of theranostic nanoparticles in cancer and other diseases, highlighting their potential to improve diagnosis and treatment outcomes through targeted delivery, imaging, and synergistic therapeutic effects.

sec.title: Exosome-based nanomedicine
sec.p: As important intercellular communication mediators, exosomes have demonstrated promise as therapeutic agents for several illnesses, such as cancer, osteoarthritis (OA), and wound healing. Their capacity to transport bioactive substances like proteins and miRNAs presents great promise for tissue regeneration and targeted treatments [332].

Cancer therapy explores exosome-based approaches to modulate the TME and enhance antitumor responses. Ginseng-derived exosome-like nanoparticles (GENs) have demonstrated active blood–brain-barrier (BBB) penetration and TME modulation, effectively recruiting M1 macrophages and inhibiting glioma progression [333]. Similarly, M1-like macrophage-derived exosomes (M1-Exos) have been integrated with aptamer-conjugated liposomes to create hybrid nanovesicles (M1E/AALs) for targeted TME reprogramming. These nanovesicles, loaded with PFTBA and IR780, alleviate tumor hypoxia, repolarize TAMs, and enhance photodynamic immunotherapy in triple-negative breast cancer models [296]. Furthermore, tea leaf-derived exosome-like nanotherapeutics (TLNTs) have demonstrated promise in retarding breast tumor growth through pro-apoptosis and microbiota modulation, demonstrating the potential of plant-derived exosome-like nanoparticles for cancer treatment [334].

In osteoarthritis, exosome-based therapies aim to rejuvenate aging chondrocytes and promote cartilage regeneration. Umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stem cell-derived exosomes (UCMSC-EXOs) have been engineered with chondrocyte-targeting polymers and encapsulated within hyaluronic acid microgels for sustained release, effectively repairing OA cartilage in rat models [335]. Additionally, chondrocyte-targeted hybrid exosomes (CAP/FGF18-hyEXO) loaded with an FGF18-targeted gene-editing tool have been encapsulated in hydrogel microspheres, demonstrating synergistic promotion of cartilage regeneration and decreased inflammation [336]. Bone marrow mesenchymal stromal cell-derived exosomes (Exo) have also been engineered with targeting peptides and encapsulated in hydrogels, enhancing targeting ability and cartilage repair in OA murine models [337].

Exosomes have demonstrated promise in wound healing and tissue regeneration. Umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cell-derived exosomes (hUCMSC-exos) combined with Pluronic F-127 hydrogel have significantly accelerated wound closure and enhanced skin regeneration in diabetic rat models [338]. Dental pulp stem cell-derived exosomes (DPSC-EXO) have demonstrated anti-inflammatory and osteogenic effects, promoting the repair of experimental periodontitis in rats [339]. Moreover, mechanical stress-induced C2 C12-derived exosomes (Exosome-MS) have shown therapeutic effects on glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis by promoting osteogenesis through the miR-92a-3p/PTEN/AKT signaling pathway [340] (Fig. 8).

sec.p: In lung diseases, exosomal STIMATE derived from type II alveolar epithelial cells can control the metabolic reprogramming of tissue-resident alveolar macrophages, suggesting potential therapeutic applications in lung injury and fibrosis [341].

As important intercellular communication mediators, exosomes can act as therapeutic agents for many diseases, such as cancer, osteoarthritis (OA), and wound healing. Their capacity to transport bioactive substances like proteins and miRNAs presents great promise for tissue regeneration and targeted treatments.

sec.title: Clinical trials
sec.p: With promising developments in drug transport, treatments, and diagnostics, nanomedicine—the use of nanotechnology in healthcare—has advanced significantly in clinical studies. Several products based on nanomedicine have already received approval for usage, and many others are currently undergoing clinical review. For example, FDA-approved liposomal formulations such as Doxil (doxorubicin) and Abraxane (paclitaxel-bound albumin nanoparticles) for the treatment of cancer have better efficacy and fewer adverse effects than traditional medicines [342].

Numerous uses of nanomedicine, such as targeted medication administration, imaging, and regenerative medicine, are being investigated in ongoing clinical trials. The potential of nanoparticles, including polymeric micelles, dendrimers, and gold nanoparticles, to improve drug solubility, stability, and bioavailability is being investigated [343]. The potential of nanomedicine to treat complicated illnesses like Alzheimer's, heart conditions, and infectious infections is also being researched. Lipid nanoparticles, for instance, are being used in mRNA-based COVID-19 vaccines, demonstrating the adaptability of nanomedicine in tackling global health issues [306].

Notwithstanding these developments, there are still issues, including scaling, regulatory barriers, and long-term safety worries. These problems are being addressed by continued research and cooperation between industry, academia, and regulatory agencies, opening the door for wider clinical usage. Clinical trials of nanomedicine appear to have a bright future ahead of them, with the potential to transform customized medicine and enhance patient outcomes everywhere. sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: The transformative potential of nanoparticle-mediated cancer immunotherapy is tempered by several critical knowledge gaps that must guide future research, including heterogeneous patient responses requiring predictive biomarkers, limited understanding of nanocarrier-induced long-term immune memory, and scalability challenges in clinical translation. To advance the field, future work should prioritize engineering adaptable nanoplatforms to overcome dynamic immune evasion, integrating AI-driven design with high-throughput screening for personalized therapies, and developing standardized preclinical models that better mimic human immune-tumor interactions. By addressing these specific challenges through interdisciplinary collaboration, researchers can bridge the gap between promising preclinical results and robust clinical applications, ultimately realizing the full potential of nanotechnology to revolutionize cancer immunotherapy and improve patient outcomes.
